Content Safety image analysis
Content Understanding video analyzer
questions.explain: New images come from generation, targeted changes from a masked edit, harm scores from Content Safety image analysis, and per-scene descriptions from a Content Understanding video analyzer.
questions.teach: Vision work in the exam splits into creating media, editing media, judging media and understanding media. Generation makes new images from prompts, editing changes a region marked by a mask, Content Safety returns harm categories with severity, and Content Understanding extracts structured descriptions from images, audio and video.
hints: For each row, decide whether it creates something new, changes something that exists, judges whether content is acceptable, or explains what content contains.
Changing one object while keeping the rest of a photo is not the same as creating from nothing: the existing pixels must be preserved outside one marked region.
Scoring for harm returns categories and severities, while describing scenes returns text about what happens. Two options are unused: one works on audio and one splits text.
questions.deep: Generated images in Foundry carry provenance metadata (C2PA content credentials), which supports the exam's 'watermarks and provenance' skill. Apply Content Safety to generated output too, not only to uploads.

questions.prompt: Your moderation rule blocks images at severity 4 or higher. Which severity values can Content Safety image analysis return?
options: Low, medium and high, with no numbers
Every integer from 0 to 7
A probability between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Image analysis returns the trimmed scale 0, 2, 4 and 6 for each category. The full 0 to 7 scale is available only for text when you request eight severity levels.
questions.teach: Content Safety scores each harm category (hate, sexual, violence, self-harm) with a severity. The text model supports the full 0 to 7 scale but returns 0, 2, 4 and 6 by default, and can return all eight levels on request. The image model supports only the trimmed scale: each pair of adjacent levels maps to one value.
hints: Severity in Content Safety is a number, not a word label and not a probability, so two of the options describe a different kind of output altogether.
The underlying scale has eight levels, but adjacent pairs are often merged into a single reported value. Think about what values remain when 0 and 1 become one value, 2 and 3 become one, and so on.
Text analysis can be asked for the finer scale; image analysis cannot. So for images you only ever see the merged values, which is why a rule at 4 works cleanly.
questions.deep: Foundry guardrails express thresholds as Low, Medium and High rather than numbers, which is why the 'low, medium, high' distractor feels familiar. The API itself returns the numeric severity.

questions.prompt: A call-centre voice agent keeps mistranscribing product names such as 'Fjellstue 2P' and 'Trollhetta'. Which two kinds of training data help a custom speech model fix this? Choose two.
options: The agent's tool JSON schemas
Plain text sentences that use the product names
Audio recordings paired with human-labelled transcripts
Product photos with alt text
SSML files that set the speaking rate
answer: Plain text sentences that use the product names
Audio recordings paired with human-labelled transcripts
questions.explain: Domain text teaches the new vocabulary, and audio with human-labelled transcripts teaches pronunciation and acoustics. Photos, SSML (a text to speech format) and tool schemas do not train recognition.
questions.teach: Custom speech adapts the speech to text base model to your domain. Plain text data teaches vocabulary and phrasing, which is cheap and fixes most unknown words. Audio with human-labelled transcripts teaches acoustics, such as accents, noise and how names are actually pronounced. You test the custom model's word error rate against the base model before deploying an endpoint.
hints: The model is turning audio into text, so useful training data must be about language or about sound. Discard anything that is about images, voices being generated, or tool definitions.
One kind of data teaches the model which words and phrases exist in your domain, without any audio at all. That alone often fixes unfamiliar product names.
The other kind pairs real recordings with exactly what was said, so the model learns how those words sound in your callers' voices and line conditions.
questions.deep: For quick wins without training, a phrase list boosts recognition of specific terms at runtime. Measure word error rate (WER) on a held-out test set to prove the custom model is better before switching traffic.

questions.prompt: A conference needs live captions of an English keynote in German, French and Norwegian at the same time. What fits best?
options: Content Understanding with the prebuilt-audioSearch analyzer
Text to speech with three neural voices
Speech translation, which recognises the English audio and returns several target languages at once
Batch transcription, then translating the transcript after the talk
answer: Speech translation, which recognises the English audio and returns several target languages at once
questions.explain: Speech translation streams recognition and returns multiple target languages at once, which suits live captions. Batch work is after the fact, TTS goes the wrong way, and audioSearch summarises recordings.
questions.teach: The Speech service offers speech to text, text to speech and speech translation. Speech translation takes source audio in real time and returns translated text in one or more target languages from the same stream, optionally with synthesized translated audio. Batch transcription is for recorded files processed later.
hints: Two words decide it: live and simultaneous. Any option that waits for the talk to end fails the first, and any option that handles one language at a time strains the second.
Generating speech from text is the opposite direction from what captions need. The input here is spoken audio, and the output is written text in other languages.
Summarising a recorded conversation for search is a different job from streaming captions while someone is speaking. Pick the capability that translates as audio arrives.
questions.deep: LLM-based translation flows are also in scope: transcribe, then translate with a prompt that enforces a glossary. That trades latency for terminology control, so it fits recorded content better than live captions.

questions.prompt: Arrange one turn of a voice-enabled agent from first to last.
tray: Convert the reply text to speech
Convert the speech to text
Stream the synthesized audio back to the caller
Capture the caller's audio
The agent reasons over the text and calls tools
answer: Capture the caller's audio
Convert the speech to text
The agent reasons over the text and calls tools
Convert the reply text to speech
Stream the synthesized audio back to the caller
questions.explain: Audio is captured, transcribed, reasoned over by the agent, synthesized back to speech and then streamed to the caller. Each step needs the previous step's output.
questions.teach: A classic voice agent is a pipeline: speech to text turns the caller's audio into text, the agent reasons and calls tools on that text, text to speech turns the reply into audio, and the audio streams back. Real-time speech-to-speech options collapse some of these steps, but the logical order of a turn stays the same.
hints: Nothing can be recognised before it is heard, and nothing can be played before it is produced. Place the first and last steps using that rule alone.
The agent's reasoning and tool calls work on text, so the caller's words must already be written down before the agent can think about them.
The agent's reply starts as text. It has to become audio before anything can be sent back to the caller's ear, so the conversion step sits just before playback.
questions.deep: Latency adds up across the chain, so stream partial recognition results and start synthesis on the first sentence of the reply. azure-ai-projects 2.7.0 added preview voice agents for real-time speech-to-speech.

questions.prompt: An app extracts supplier name, invoice total and due date from emails with a language model, and downstream code crashes when a field is missing or misnamed. Which two changes make it reliable? Choose two.
options: Remove the field descriptions from the schema to save tokens
Define the fields in a strict JSON schema and use structured outputs
Raise the temperature so the model explores more phrasings
Validate the parsed result in code and send failures to review or retry
End the prompt with 'please reply in valid JSON'
answer: Define the fields in a strict JSON schema and use structured outputs
Validate the parsed result in code and send failures to review or retry
questions.explain: Structured outputs with a strict schema enforce field names and required fields, and code validation catches wrong values. Polite requests, higher temperature and thinner schemas make failures more likely.
questions.teach: Language models can extract entities and fields into JSON, but free-form JSON drifts: fields go missing or get renamed. Structured outputs constrain generation to a JSON schema you supply, so required fields and names are enforced. Code-side validation remains the safety net for values that are well-formed but wrong.
hints: Separate two failure types: the shape of the output is wrong, or the shape is right but a value is wrong. A robust design handles both, with one mechanism for each.
Asking politely for JSON is a request, not a guarantee. Look for the option that makes the model's output conform to a declared structure.
More randomness makes field names less stable, and stripping field descriptions removes hints the model uses to fill fields correctly. Both move in the wrong direction.
questions.deep: For fixed document types (invoices, receipts), Content Understanding or Document Intelligence prebuilt models return typed fields with confidence and grounding, which is often better than prompting a chat model.

questions.prompt: A forum policy needs a finer severity scale than the four values this code prints. Which change returns all eight severity levels?
questions.code:
from azure.ai.contentsafety import ContentSafetyClient
from azure.ai.contentsafety.models import AnalyzeTextOptions
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

client = ContentSafetyClient(ENDPOINT, DefaultAzureCredential())
result = client.analyze_text(AnalyzeTextOptions(text=comment))
for item in result.categories_analysis:
    print(item.category, item.severity)
options: Read item.score instead of item.severity
Call client.analyze_image instead of analyze_text
Pass halt_on_blocklist_hit=True to AnalyzeTextOptions
Pass output_type="EightSeverityLevels" to AnalyzeTextOptions
answer: Pass output_type="EightSeverityLevels" to AnalyzeTextOptions
questions.explain: output_type="EightSeverityLevels" makes text analysis return 0 to 7 instead of 0, 2, 4, 6. Blocklist settings, image analysis and a nonexistent score field do not change the scale.
questions.teach: ContentSafetyClient.analyze_text takes an AnalyzeTextOptions request and returns categories_analysis: one entry per harm category with a severity. By default text severities come back as 0, 2, 4 or 6. AnalyzeTextOptions also accepts blocklist names for custom term lists and an output type that switches to the full eight-level scale.
hints: The change belongs in the request, because the service decides which scale to return before the response reaches your loop. Look at options that add something to the request object.
Blocklists deal with custom banned terms and whether to stop at the first match; they do not change how severity is reported for the harm categories.
Analysing images uses the trimmed scale only, and there is no score attribute that secretly holds finer values. The option you want names the output format explicitly.
questions.deep: The enum form is AnalyzeTextOutputType.EIGHT_SEVERITY_LEVELS. ContentSafetyClient accepts AzureKeyCredential or an Entra credential such as DefaultAzureCredential; with Entra you need a custom subdomain endpoint and the Cognitive Services User role.

questions.prompt: A retailer must translate 40,000 Word manuals into five languages, keep the formatting, and always render its brand terms the same way. Which option fits?
options: Azure Translator document translation with a glossary
A language model prompt per page with no terminology list
Speech translation on a narrated version of each manual
Content Understanding with the prebuilt-layout analyzer
answer: Azure Translator document translation with a glossary
questions.explain: Document translation handles whole Word files in bulk while preserving formatting, and a glossary enforces brand terms. Speech, ad hoc prompts and layout extraction miss one or more requirements.
questions.teach: Azure Translator offers text translation for strings and document translation for whole files. Document translation keeps the source structure and formatting (Word, PDF, slides) and runs asynchronously over storage containers, which suits large batches. Glossaries pin how specific terms are translated, so brand and product names stay consistent.
hints: Three requirements: very large volume of files, formatting preserved, and fixed terminology. A per-page prompt meets none of the three well, especially the last one.
Speech is about audio, and nothing here is spoken. Layout extraction reads structure out of documents but does not translate anything.
Look for a translation service mode that takes whole files rather than strings, plus a feature that fixes how named terms are translated.
questions.deep: LLM-powered translation flows are also in the outline; they shine for tone or domain adaptation, but you must supply terminology in the prompt and handle formatting yourself. Custom Translator trains domain models when glossaries are not enough.

questions.prompt: What kind of query does this code send, and how are the result lists combined?
questions.code:
vector_query = VectorizedQuery(
    vector=embed("lightweight tent for windy ridges"),
    k_nearest_neighbors=5,
    fields="contentVector",
)
results = search_client.search(
    search_text="lightweight tent windy ridge",
    vector_queries=[vector_query],
    top=5,
)
options: Pure vector; search_text is ignored when vector_queries is set
Hybrid; keyword and vector results are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
Two separate queries whose results the client must merge
Semantic; the vector re-ranks the keyword results
answer: Hybrid; keyword and vector results are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
questions.explain: Sending search_text and vector_queries together is a hybrid query, and the service fuses the BM25 and vector rankings with RRF. Semantic ranking needs query_type set, and nothing is merged client-side.
questions.teach: Azure AI Search supports keyword (BM25) search on searchable text fields, vector search on vector fields, and hybrid search, which runs both in one request and merges the ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Semantic ranking is a separate, optional step that re-ranks the top results with a language model and can add captions and answers.
hints: Count how many kinds of input the request carries. There is a plain text string and there is a vector query. A request carrying both kinds is the defining feature of one query type.
Both inputs go into one search call, and one result set comes back. So the service, not your code, must be combining two ranked lists into one.

Semantic re-ranking is switched on by its own parameter, which this code does not set. The merge algorithm used here works on ranks, not raw scores, so lists on different scales can be combined fairly.
questions.deep: VectorizedQuery takes a vector you computed; VectorizableTextQuery lets the service vectorize the text with the index's vectorizer. Hybrid plus semantic ranking is the combination Microsoft's own relevance tests rank highest for RAG.

questions.prompt: Semantic ranker is enabled on the service, and the index has a semantic configuration named manuals-semantic. What must you add to this call to get semantically re-ranked results?
questions.code:
results = search_client.search(
    search_text="boots that stay dry in snow",
    top=10,
)
options: vector_queries=[VectorizedQuery(...)] and nothing else
filter="semantic eq true"
query_type="semantic" and semantic_configuration_name="manuals-semantic"
query_language="en-us" and nothing else
answer: query_type="semantic" and semantic_configuration_name="manuals-semantic"
questions.explain: query_type="semantic" turns on re-ranking and semantic_configuration_name picks which configuration's fields to use. Vectors, a language hint or a filter do not invoke the semantic ranker.
questions.teach: Semantic ranking is opt-in per request. The index holds a semantic configuration that names the title, content and keyword fields the ranker should read. A query asks for it by setting the query type to semantic and naming the configuration; the service then re-ranks the top keyword or hybrid results with a language understanding model.
hints: Enabling the ranker on the service and defining a configuration in the index are both prerequisites. The query itself still has to ask for semantic ranking explicitly.
An index can hold several semantic configurations, so the request has to say which one to use. Look for the option that both switches the mode and names the configuration.
Adding a vector query makes the request hybrid, not semantic. A language hint alone changes nothing about ranking, and filters only narrow results by field values.
questions.deep: If the index defines a default semantic configuration you can omit the name, but naming it is explicit and exam-safe. Semantic ranking also returns captions and answers when you request them.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the index field attribute that enables it.
rows: Restrict results to category eq 'boots'
Order results by price, lowest first
Show a count of products per brand in a sidebar
Match words the user types inside the description
options: filterable
searchable
sortable
facetable
key
answer: filterable
sortable
facetable
searchable
questions.explain: Filters need filterable, ordering needs sortable, per-value counts need facetable, and full-text matching needs searchable. The key attribute only identifies documents.
questions.teach: Every field in an Azure AI Search index carries attributes that decide what queries can do with it. Searchable fields are analysed for full-text search, filterable fields support $filter expressions, sortable fields support $orderby, facetable fields return counts per value, and exactly one string field is the document key. Attributes cost storage, so enable only what you use.
hints: Read each row for the query operation it describes: excluding documents, ordering them, counting them by value, or matching words inside text.
Excluding documents by an exact value and ordering them by a value are two different operations, each with its own attribute, even though both read the same kind of field.
Counting products per brand is what powers the sidebar navigation on shopping sites. One option is unused: it identifies each document uniquely rather than enabling a query feature.
questions.deep: Changing most attributes on an existing field requires rebuilding the index, so plan them up front. In the Python SDK, SearchableField sets searchable by default while SimpleField is for filter, sort and facet use.

questions.prompt: Match each indexing or query need to the Azure AI Search feature that handles it.
rows: Make a search for 'cheval' also match the French plural 'chevaux'
Read printed text from scanned pages during indexing
Tag part numbers using your own Azure Function
Turn each chunk into a vector during indexing
options: Azure OpenAI Embedding skill
Key Phrase Extraction skill
OCR skill
A French language analyzer on the field
Shaper skill
Custom Web API skill
answer: A French language analyzer on the field
OCR skill
Custom Web API skill
Azure OpenAI Embedding skill
questions.explain: Stemming is a language analyzer's job, OCR reads scanned text, Custom Web API calls your Function, and the Azure OpenAI Embedding skill vectorizes chunks during indexing.
questions.teach: Analyzers and skills work at different stages. An analyzer processes text in searchable fields, at indexing and query time, breaking it into tokens and normalising them (for example stemming French plurals). Skills run in a skillset during indexing to enrich content: built-in skills such as OCR or Azure OpenAI Embedding, and custom skills such as Custom Web API, which calls your own endpoint.
hints: First decide for each row whether it changes how words are tokenised and matched, or whether it adds new content during indexing. The first kind is an analyzer, the second kind is a skill.
Matching singular and plural word forms in one language is a linguistic rule applied to text in a field. Reading scanned pages and generating vectors add new data to the enriched document instead.
When the logic is yours and runs in an Azure Function, the skill must call out to your endpoint over HTTP. Two options are unused: one reshapes data, one extracts key phrases.
questions.deep: Analyzers are set per field and mostly cannot change on an existing field without a rebuild. Built-in Foundry Tools skills use your attached Foundry resource for billing only, while the embedding skill calls your own deployment for processing.

questions.prompt: A team ingests mixed PDFs, slide decks and scanned forms into a RAG index. They want clean Markdown with tables preserved, descriptions of charts and diagrams, and chunks ready for embedding, with no custom model training. What should they use?
options: A Document Intelligence custom extraction model trained on labelled samples
Content Safety text analysis on each page
The Text Split skill applied to the raw PDF bytes
Content Understanding with the prebuilt-documentSearch analyzer
answer: Content Understanding with the prebuilt-documentSearch analyzer
questions.explain: prebuilt-documentSearch outputs layout-aware Markdown, figure descriptions and embedding-ready chunks with no training. A custom extraction model needs labelled data, and the other options produce no usable content.
questions.teach: Document Intelligence and Content Understanding overlap on OCR and layout but aim at different jobs. Document Intelligence centres on extracting fields, tables and layout from documents, with prebuilt and custom trained models. Content Understanding uses generative models across modalities and returns grounded Markdown or schema JSON, and its prebuilt-documentSearch analyzer is built for RAG ingestion, including figure descriptions and chunking.
hints: Note the words 'no custom model training'. Any option that starts with labelling samples to train a model breaks that constraint, however accurate it might become.
Describing a chart in words requires a model that interprets images, not one that only reads characters. Splitting raw file bytes produces chunks of binary noise, not Markdown.
Safety analysis scores harm and produces no content for an index. Look for the analyzer whose stated purpose is preparing documents for retrieval-augmented generation.
questions.deep: Rule of thumb: fixed forms where you need specific fields, think Document Intelligence or a Content Understanding domain analyzer; content for an agent or RAG to reason over, think Content Understanding Markdown. Content Understanding is also a skill in Azure AI Search.

questions.prompt: After adding an Azure OpenAI Embedding skill to the skillset, only documents changed since the last run receive vectors. Which call is missing before run_indexer so every document is reprocessed?
options: indexer_client.reset_indexer("manuals-indexer")
indexer_client.create_data_source_connection(data_source)
search_client.upload_documents(documents=[])
indexer_client.get_indexer_status("manuals-indexer")
answer: indexer_client.reset_indexer("manuals-indexer")
questions.explain: reset_indexer clears the indexer's change-tracking state so run_indexer reprocesses every document with the new skill. Status reads, a new data source and an empty upload leave the high-water mark in place.
questions.teach: Indexers track a high-water mark through change detection, so a normal run only processes new or changed source documents. When you change the skillset, unchanged documents are skipped and never get the new enrichment. Resetting the indexer clears its change-tracking state so the next run processes everything again.
hints: The symptom is that unchanged documents are skipped. Ask what the indexer remembers between runs that makes it skip them, and how you would make it forget.
Reading the indexer's status tells you what happened but changes nothing. Creating another data source connection points at the same blobs and does not clear any memory.
Uploading an empty list of documents to the index does nothing to the indexer's own tracking. The answer is a call on the indexer client that clears its state.
questions.deep: On large indexes a full reset is expensive; enrichment caching with incremental enrichment can reprocess only the skills that changed. Also remember that a run can report success while individual documents fail within maxFailedItems; get_indexer_status returns the execution history with per-document errors.
